svg.text: # tidx = 0: thread 0, one of the block's 128
grey: lanes 4–31, the same pattern on other rows and keys
The code starts by picking one thread, tidx, of the
block's 128. Thread 0 is lane 0 of warp 0, and warp 0 has
get_slice returns a rule, not data: which spots of each
instruction's Q, K and S pieces this lane holds. Choosing
the instruction in idea 2 fixed that table. NVIDIA defines
it and CuTe has it built in; no line of our code spells it
Lanes 1–3, the rest of quad 0, fill in rows 0 and 8 (key 0
of K), two neighbouring columns each: a 32-bit register
holds two bf16 values. Quad 1 does rows 1 and 9, and so
on, as in “What is a warp, a lane and a quad?”.

svg.text: partition_A cuts the Q tile into the instruction's 16 × 16
pieces and keeps thread 0's 8 spots in each: rows 0 and 8,
dims +0, +1, +8, +9, as in step 1. Only warp 0's rows
count, so that is 1 piece down and 4 across.
It copies nothing. tSsQ only records where these 32 values
CuTe prints the shape as ((2, 2, 2), 1, 4): the 8 split
into pair × row 0 or 8 × dims +0 or +8.

svg.text: partition_B does the same for K. A K piece is 8 keys × 16
dims, so the tile is 8 pieces down and 4 across. In each,
thread 0 has the first key, dims +0, +1, +8, +9.
Why 128 values, against 32 of Q? Every warp scores its own
rows against all 64 keys, so K is not split between warps.

the shapes of tSsQ and tSsK. They stay empty until the
acc_S is thread 0's part of the score tile S: rows 0 and
8, keys +0 and +1 of each 16 × 8 S piece. The kernel
zeroes it before each key block.

svg.text: S[0, 0] after each step sums head dims:
Step k takes piece column k of both shapes: head dims 16k
to 16k + 15. In [None, None, k], None keeps a whole mode,
like : in NumPy, and k picks one piece across.
① ② copy those values from shared memory into the same
③ gemm runs 8 instructions, one per K piece n: Q piece k
with K piece n, added into S piece n of acc_S. Each runs
on the whole warp; thread 0 brings only its spots, and
lanes 1–3 the rest of each row (step 1).
acc_S is both input and output, so the steps add up: after
k = 3 every score sums all 64 head dims.
